name: Friedrich Nietzsche
summary: Nietzsche wrote against democracy, socialism, equality, Christianity and the modern state, and in favour of a higher type of person, struggle and war. He was openly critical of German nationalism and of antisemitism, and his sister's posthumous editing (The Will to Power) presented him with views that his published writings do not state.

state-harmful.rationale: In Zarathustra's 'On the New Idol' the state is called 'the coldest of all cold monsters', a lie that devised 'the superfluous ones', and a thing to be rejected as an idol.

nation-first.rationale: Inferred: he mocks 'Germany above all' and the nationalist 'folly' of his countrymen and calls for 'good Europeans' rather than loyalty to a single nation.

revolution-justified.rationale: Mixed: he derides socialist revolution as resentment and the Commune as a primitive reversion, yet he calls for a revaluation of all values that he describes in revolutionary terms.

democracy-best.rationale: Beyond Good and Evil calls the democratic movement 'a degenerating form of political organization', and Twilight calls modern democracy 'a decaying form of the State' and 'the death agony' of organised power.

direct-votes.rationale: Inferred: from his critique of democratic majority rule and the democratic taste as a decline of the higher type; he never discusses referendums.

natural-rulers.rationale: Beyond Good and Evil and Zarathustra describe a higher type of man and an aristocratic order that should command, against levelling; he says the higher type is 'the most feared' and must be willed.

political-violence-never.rationale: Inferred: his praise of war as sanctifying a cause and of the 'good war' rejects a blanket ban on violence, but he never discusses political violence in general.

war-builds-character.rationale: Zarathustra says 'it is the good war which halloweth every cause', and Twilight calls war the great policy of the deep spirit and says the man who has renounced war has renounced a grand life.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Contested: he calls a 'nation' a young res facta rather than a race and says Europe's peoples are not yet a race, but he also describes a noble racial lineage.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Inferred: from his rejection of the levelling of rank and of the universal, green-meadow happiness of the herd; equality of outcomes as such is not addressed.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Inferred: he attacks altruism and sympathy as signs of decline and calls for self-overcoming, which follows from treating one's own strength as the measure of value.

conscription.rationale: In the Genealogy he calls universal military service an antidote to 'the effeminacy of democratic ideas', which is support for compulsory service.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: He holds that all knowing is perspectival and that what is called objective or scientific reflects the values and interests of the one who knows; this matches the claim that knowledge reflects who holds power.

universal-morality.rationale: Beyond Good and Evil states that 'there is no such thing as moral phenomena, but only a moral interpretation of phenomena', so he denies that moral truths hold across all cultures and eras.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He treats Socratic reason = virtue = happiness as a decadent idiosyncrasy and ranks instinct above rationality, so reason is not the sole guide for him.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: He describes women's 'first and last function' as bearing robust children and wants women to keep their 'eternally feminine' character rather than adopt men's roles.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: A single remark in Beyond Good and Evil ties depression to 'the crossing of too heterogeneous races'; he does not propose any restriction on marriage or children.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He calls the 'equality of men' a doctrine to be unlearned and 'preachers of equality' 'tarantulas'; he also calls 'equality before the law' a vulgar levelling against the privileged and autocratic.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: He tells readers to 'live in war with your equals and with yourselves' and holds that struggle and inequality between individuals and peoples drive the rise of higher types.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Gay Science and Zarathustra praise individuality, becoming who one is, and the free spirit against custom and the herd, which fits encouraging eccentric ways of living.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: In Beyond Good and Evil he says that Jews 'COULD' seize supremacy over Europe but are 'NOT working and planning for that end', and he calls anti-Semitic agitation a folly and a sign of national sickness.

religion-illusion.rationale: He treats Christian belief as a product of suffering, decadence and the priests' remedy for weakness, and announces that God is dead, though he does not predict that religion will fade with better material conditions.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: He argues that women's economic and legal independence as clerks, and the 'emancipation of woman', weakened women's most womanly instincts and were a symptom of decline.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: He declares 'God is dead' and treats the law of God as a priestly means of power over men, so he rejects the claim that rulers answer to divine law.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Inferred: he praises war, military virtue and soldierliness and never suggests a country could do without an army.

person-over-state.rationale: Contested: he is hostile to the state as an idol and sees the individual's strength as the measure of value, but he also tells rulers to subordinate persons to a common order.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Zarathustra tells his hearers to love peace only as a means to new wars, and that a good war sanctifies any cause; he rejects confining force to defence.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Inferred: he contrasts religions by their values and sees Christianity as one decadent form among others rather than one shared truth.

women-suffrage.rationale: Inferred: he criticises lowering women to 'newspaper reading and meddling with politics' and opposes women's claims to rights; he never mentions the vote itself.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: In The Antichrist he calls the Bible's treatment of Israel a priestly 'falsification' and says the scriptures are the work of priests; he holds no literal or inerrant reading.

notes: Answers rest on his own published books, read as full text; aphorisms are ironic and sometimes voice opposing views, so ambiguous passages are low or 0. The Will to Power (edited by his sister) was not used. Many statements are null because his writings do not address them. Salience was not considered when answering.
